title: Life Insurance Product Types: A Comprehensive Survey

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Describe all major types of term assurance — level, decreasing, increasing, return-of-premium, renewable, and convertible — and identify the circumstances in which each is most appropriate.
Explain the structure and actuarial logic of whole life assurance, distinguishing between ordinary whole life, limited-payment, and single-premium variants.
Describe endowment assurance in all its forms: conventional, pure endowment, educational endowment, and the anticipated endowment (money-back policy) that dominates the Nigerian retail market.
Explain universal life and variable (investment-linked) life assurance, including their flexibility features, investment risks, and Nigerian regulatory treatment.
Describe joint-life and last-survivor policies and explain their key applications in Nigerian practice.
Identify and explain the main life assurance riders: critical illness, total and permanent disability, waiver of premium, accidental death benefit, and hospital cash.
Explain keyman insurance and its application to business protection in Nigeria.
Describe mortgage protection and credit life insurance, including NIIRA 2025's mandatory credit life provision for loans exceeding ₦10 million.
Analyse the Nigerian life insurance product landscape, identifying the dominant products by market segment.
Apply product suitability principles to match life insurance products to specific client circumstances.

blocks.text: 6.1  Introduction: The Product Universe of Life Insurance

blocks.h: Life insurance is not a single product — it is a product universe. Within that universe, products vary along at least five dimensions simultaneously: the certainty of the benefit payment (term vs whole life); the presence or absence of a savings element (protection-only vs savings-and-protection); the beneficiary of the payment (death benefit vs survival benefit vs maturity benefit); the flexibility of the premium and benefit structure (rigid vs adjustable); and the investment risk borne by the policyholder (guaranteed vs market-linked). Understanding how these dimensions interact, and how different products position themselves within this multi-dimensional space, is the foundation of competent life insurance practice.

This chapter provides a comprehensive survey of every major product type in the Nigerian and international life insurance market. It is structured to move from the simplest to the most complex: beginning with term assurance, proceeding through whole life and endowment variants, addressing the hybrid and flexible products (universal life, investment-linked), and then examining the special-purpose products (joint-life, keyman, credit life, mortgage protection) that serve specific client needs in the Nigerian market. Each product type is examined through four lenses: its structure and mechanics, its actuarial logic, its strengths and limitations, and its applications in Nigeria.

blocks.title: Nigerian Market — The Nigerian Life Product Landscape — Overview

blocks.h: The Nigerian retail life insurance market is characterised by the dominance of savings-and-protection hybrid products — principally the anticipated endowment ('money-back policy') and the educational endowment plan. Pure term assurance, while growing in market share, remains underpenetrated relative to comparable markets. Investment-linked products are emerging, led by AXA Mansard's Wealth Plus, Leadway's Smart Life, and similar offerings from ARM Life and Stanbic IBTC Insurance. The group life market is driven by the Pension Reform Act 2014's mandatory employer scheme obligation. The annuity market is growing as the Contributory Pension Scheme matures and retirees exercise their RLA purchase right.
Key product market data from NairaCompare's 2026 analysis of Nigerian insurers:

items.h: AXA Mansard: Agusto & Co 'Aa' rating; ₦650+ billion AUM (largest in Nigeria); leading products — Educate (education insurance), Future Plus (endowment), Wealth Plus (unit-linked, returned 14% in 2024).

Leadway Assurance: Agusto & Co 'A' rating; ₦320 billion AUM; leading products — Future Assure (education, minimum ₦10,000/month), Leadway Wealth (endowment, 11% average 5-year return), Smart Life (unit-linked).
Other significant players: Stanbic IBTC Insurance, ARM Life, Custodian Life, African Alliance Insurance, AIICO Insurance, Cornerstone Insurance, NEM Insurance.

blocks.h: Term assurance is the purest and simplest form of life insurance: the insurer undertakes to pay the sum assured if the life assured dies within a defined period (the 'term'), and pays nothing if the life assured survives to the end of the term. There is no savings element, no maturity benefit, and no cash value. Term assurance is insurance in its most elemental form — the transfer of a contingent financial risk (the risk of death during a specific period) in exchange for a premium.

The actuarial logic of term assurance is straightforward. The insurer needs to collect, in aggregate, enough premium from all policyholders in a given age and risk cohort to cover the expected deaths in that cohort during the term, plus expenses and profit. Because most policyholders will survive the term and pay no claim, the premium per unit of cover is low — dramatically lower than whole life or endowment premiums for the same sum assured. This cost efficiency makes term assurance the most economical route to high levels of life cover for families and businesses with limited insurance budgets.

A life insurance policy providing a death benefit (the sum assured) payable only if the life assured dies within a specified period (the policy term). If the life assured survives to the end of the term, no benefit is paid and the policy expires. Term assurance has no savings element, no cash value, and no surrender value. It is the most cost-efficient form of life cover per unit of protection.
Cf: Whole life assurance (cover for the entire lifetime; certain payment) and endowment assurance (cover for a fixed term with a maturity benefit if the insured survives).
(a) Level Term Assurance

Level term assurance is the standard and most widely sold form of term insurance. The sum assured remains constant throughout the policy term, and the premium is fixed for the duration of the policy at inception. <sup>[1]</sup> If a policyholder takes out a 20-year level term policy with a sum assured of ₦10 million, the death benefit is ₦10 million whether death occurs in year 1 or year 19 of the term. The premium does not increase during the policy term even as the policyholder ages, because the premium is calculated at inception to be actuarially adequate for the full term on a level basis.

Level term is the most appropriate product for general income replacement — covering the financial risk of the breadwinner's premature death for the years during which dependants are most financially vulnerable. In Nigeria, a 20- or 25-year level term policy taken out at the birth of a child, with a sum assured calibrated to replace the breadwinner's income for the family's most dependent years, is the most cost-efficient structure for family protection.
(b) Decreasing Term Assurance

In decreasing term assurance, the sum assured declines over the policy term — typically in a straight-line (linear) reduction or on a curve mirroring the reducing balance of a loan. The premium is level throughout, even as the benefit decreases. Decreasing term is designed for situations where the financial obligation that the insurance is protecting also decreases over time, principally mortgage debt.<sup>[2]</sup>

A common application is mortgage protection: a homeowner with a ₦30 million 20-year mortgage takes out a ₦30 million 20-year decreasing term policy. If the life assured dies in year 1, the sum assured is approximately ₦30 million (matching the full outstanding mortgage). If death occurs in year 15, the sum assured has reduced to approximately ₦7.5 million (matching the reduced outstanding balance). The family never receives more than the mortgage liability requires — and the insurer prices the reducing benefit at a lower total cost than an equivalent level term policy.
(c) Increasing Term Assurance

Increasing term assurance is the reverse: the sum assured grows over the policy term, typically by a fixed percentage per year or indexed to inflation. The purpose is to maintain the real value of the death benefit in an inflationary environment. In Nigeria, where the CPI has averaged well above 20% annually in recent years, an increasing term policy — or a level term policy with an annual increase clause — provides protection against the erosion of the benefit's purchasing power.

Increasing term is commonly offered as a rider on a permanent policy rather than as a standalone product. The premium necessarily increases as the benefit increases, making this form more expensive in absolute terms but more appropriate where inflation protection is a priority.
(d) Return-of-Premium Term Assurance

Return-of-premium (ROP) term assurance is a variant in which the insurer refunds the total premiums paid (without interest) if the life assured survives to the end of the term. The product addresses the objection — common in Nigerian retail selling — that term insurance 'throws money away' if no claim is made. In exchange for eliminating this objection, the policyholder pays a significantly higher premium than for standard term cover (typically 30–50% more), because the insurer must now price in a liability on survival as well as death.

ROP term is commercially successful in markets where policyholders resist buying products with no visible savings element. In Nigeria, the anticipated endowment (money-back policy) serves much the same market psychology more efficiently — it combines survival benefits with death cover in a more structured way. ROP term is less common in the Nigerian market but may gain traction as financial literacy improves and the actuarial trade-off becomes better understood.
(e) Renewable Term Assurance

A renewable term policy includes a clause giving the policyholder the right to renew the policy at the end of the term for a further period, without providing fresh evidence of insurability. This means a policyholder who has developed a health condition during the initial term can still renew — the insurer cannot decline the renewal or impose additional premiums based on the changed health status. The premium on renewal is, however, recalculated at the policyholder's then-current age, so premiums increase on each renewal.<sup>[3]</sup>

The renewable feature is valuable for policyholders who are uncertain about their long-term insurance needs — it provides optionality without committing to the higher premium of a whole life or longer-term product. The limitation is that premiums increase at each renewal, and eventually the escalating cost may make the product unaffordable. Renewable term is a short-to-medium term solution, not a lifetime protection strategy.
(f) Convertible Term Assurance

A convertible term policy gives the policyholder the right to convert the policy to a permanent product — whole life or endowment — without providing fresh medical evidence of insurability. The conversion right must be exercised before the term expires and typically before the policyholder reaches a specified age (commonly 60 or 65). The premium on the new permanent policy is set at the policyholder's age at the time of conversion, not at their original entry age.<sup>[3]</sup>

The convertible feature is strategically important. A 35-year-old who wants lifetime cover but cannot yet afford the premium of a whole life policy can start with affordable term cover and convert to whole life when their income grows — without any medical re-assessment. This eliminates the risk that their health deteriorates in the intervening period and they become uninsurable at whole life rates. In Nigerian practice, the convertible term structure provides an important entry point for young professionals who will eventually need permanent cover.

blocks.h: Whole life assurance provides life cover for the entire lifetime of the life assured — there is no fixed policy term, and the policy does not expire while premiums are paid. The sum assured is payable on death regardless of when death occurs: year 1, year 40, or year 80. Because death is certain (the question is only when), the insurer's obligation to pay is also certain, and the premium must be sufficient to fund this certainty over the policy's lifetime.<sup>[5]</sup>

The actuarial logic of whole life premiums differs fundamentally from term assurance. In term assurance, the premium needs only to cover the expected deaths within the specified period. In whole life, the premium must cover all deaths — which is every policyholder, at some point. The premium is therefore significantly higher than an equivalent term policy. However, because the policyholder pays the same premium from inception until death (or until the premium-paying period ends), the premium in the early years is higher than the current mortality cost, and the insurer builds a policy reserve (cash value) that funds the shortfall between the level premium and the rising cost of mortality in later years.

This reserve-building is the mechanism that creates the cash value of whole life policies — the accumulated difference between premiums collected and mortality costs charged, net of expenses and investment returns. The cash value grows over time and forms the basis for surrender values and policy loans.

A life assurance policy providing lifetime death benefit cover, with no fixed policy term. The sum assured is payable on death whenever it occurs, as long as the policy is in force. Whole life policies accumulate a cash value over time, available as a surrender value, policy loan collateral, or paid-up policy. The premium is higher than an equivalent term policy but remains level over the premium-paying period.
Cf: Term assurance (cover for a fixed period only; no cash value). Whole life assurance is a permanent product; term assurance is a temporary product.
(a) Ordinary (Level Premium) Whole Life

Ordinary whole life — the most common and simplest whole life structure — requires the policyholder to pay a level premium throughout their lifetime (or until the policy matures at a defined advanced age, typically 100 or 105 years). The premium is calculated at inception based on the life assured's age, health, and sex, and does not increase. The policy builds cash value gradually, accelerating in later years as the premium income increasingly exceeds the net cost of insurance.

In Nigeria, ordinary whole life is available from most major life insurers. Its principal appeal is simplicity and certainty: fixed premium, certain death benefit, no maturity risk. Its principal limitation is premium affordability in the early years relative to an equivalent term policy — a 30-year-old male paying ₦50,000 per year for ₦500,000 of whole life cover could, for the same premium, buy ₦2.5 million to ₦5 million of term cover. The trade-off between permanent cover and coverage quantum is the central product selection decision.
(b) Limited-Payment Whole Life

Limited-payment whole life compresses the premium-paying period into a defined shorter period — 10, 15, or 20 years — while maintaining lifetime cover. The life assured pays higher premiums during the premium-paying years but has no payment obligation after the payment period ends. The policy remains fully in force for the rest of the life assured's life, and the death benefit is payable whenever death occurs.<sup>[6]</sup>

Limited-payment whole life has particular appeal for professionals who expect their income-earning years to be finite — they wish to pay off the 'insurance mortgage' during their productive years and carry the policy into retirement without any further cash outflow. A 40-year-old who takes out a 20-payment whole life policy will have fully funded their lifetime cover by age 60, entering retirement with a paid-up life policy requiring no further premiums. The policy's cash value is also higher at the end of the payment period than under ordinary whole life, because the higher premiums have built the reserve faster.
(c) Single-Premium Whole Life

Single-premium whole life is a limited-payment policy taken to its logical extreme: the policyholder pays the entire premium as one lump sum at inception, and the policy is fully funded for life from that single payment. No further premiums are ever due. The policy immediately acquires a significant cash value. It is typically used as an estate planning tool — a high-net-worth individual makes a single large investment that provides an immediate guaranteed death benefit for their estate, while the cash value can be accessed through policy loans if needed.<sup>[9]</sup>

In Nigeria, single-premium whole life is not a mass-market product — it requires a substantial initial outlay and is most appropriate for HNI clients looking to transfer wealth to the next generation tax-efficiently. NAICOM product approval is required for any single-premium structure; the pricing must demonstrate actuarial adequacy at the point of the single payment. Single-premium policies may qualify as modified endowment contracts with specific tax and regulatory treatment in some jurisdictions.

As discussed in Chapter 5, whole life policies may be issued on a participating (with-profit) or non-participating (without-profit) basis. A participating whole life policy earns annual reversionary bonuses from the insurer's surplus fund, increasing the death benefit payable over time. A non-participating policy has a fixed, guaranteed death benefit with no bonus additions. The participating variant carries a higher premium but provides a growing benefit; the non-participating variant is lower-cost but provides no growth beyond the guaranteed sum.

In the Nigerian market, participating whole life is more common among the major established life insurers. The participating feature makes the product more commercially attractive as a savings vehicle — the policyholder knows the guaranteed death benefit is growing. However, the non-guaranteed nature of the bonus must always be disclosed. A policyholder who receives an illustration showing the policy's death benefit growing to ₦10 million by age 70 must understand that this projection includes non-guaranteed bonuses that could be lower if the insurer's investment returns disappoint.

Endowment assurance combines life assurance with a savings plan in a single contract. It provides a death benefit (if the life assured dies during the policy term) and a maturity benefit (if the life assured survives to the end of the term). The policyholder therefore cannot 'lose': either they or their beneficiaries receive the sum assured, plus any accumulated bonuses in a participating policy. The dual outcome — payment on death or survival, whichever occurs first — is the defining feature of endowment assurance and the source of its actuarial logic.<sup>[10]</sup>

The endowment premium is higher than either a term assurance premium (which pays only on death) or a savings product of equivalent value (which has no mortality cost). The endowment policyholder is paying for two simultaneous outputs: protection and savings. The proportion of the premium allocable to each depends on the policyholder's age, the policy term, and the sum assured. A young life on a long-term endowment has a low mortality cost and a high savings component; an older life on a short-term endowment has a higher mortality cost eating into the savings accumulation.

A life assurance policy that pays the sum assured either on the death of the life assured during the policy term or on the survival of the life assured to the end of the policy term, whichever occurs first. It combines a savings element (accumulated towards a maturity lump sum) with a protection element (death cover throughout the term). The maturity benefit is the sum assured plus, in participating policies, all accrued reversionary bonuses and any terminal bonus.

Note: Endowment assurance is more expensive than equivalent term cover because it funds both the protection and the savings elements. The savings element is the source of its appeal; the higher premium is the source of its affordability challenge for mass-market clients.
(a) Conventional (With-Profit) Endowment

The conventional or traditional endowment is a participating policy in which the guaranteed sum assured at maturity or death is supplemented by annual reversionary bonuses and a terminal bonus. This is the most common endowment structure in the Nigerian market. The policyholder knows at inception the minimum (the guaranteed sum assured) and can track the projected maturity value through annual bonus statements. The actual maturity value will exceed the guaranteed sum assured if bonuses are maintained, providing the policyholder with a share of the insurer's investment returns.

Conventional endowments are widely sold by all major Nigerian life insurers as general savings and education funding vehicles. Typical policy terms in Nigeria range from 10 to 25 years. The minimum premium entry points vary by insurer but are generally accessible at the middle-income level — from approximately ₦2,000 to ₦5,000 per month for a modest sum assured.
(b) Pure Endowment

A pure endowment is an endowment policy that pays only if the life assured survives to the maturity date. No death benefit is paid if the life assured dies before maturity — the policy simply ends without payment on death. The pure endowment is therefore the inverse of term assurance (which pays only on death). Its purpose is pure savings accumulation, not protection.<sup>[11]</sup>

Pure endowments are rarely sold as standalone retail products in Nigeria because of their obvious vulnerability: a policyholder who dies before maturity loses all the premiums paid without any benefit to dependants. However, pure endowments are an important building block in actuarial calculations and appear embedded within more complex products. An annuity contract is, at its core, a series of pure endowments.
(c) Educational Endowment (Education Insurance)

The educational endowment is an endowment policy designed specifically to fund a child's education. The policy is taken out on a parent's life with the child as the beneficiary. The maturity date is typically set to coincide with the year the child is expected to enter university or a higher institution. The maturity benefit provides the lump sum needed for tuition fees, accommodation, and living expenses.

A critical feature of educational endowments is the premium waiver rider — a provision that waives all future premiums if the policyholder (the parent or breadwinner) dies or becomes permanently disabled before the policy matures. This rider ensures the policy remains in force and the child still receives the full maturity benefit even if the parent is no longer alive to pay premiums. Without a premium waiver, the policy would lapse on the parent's death, defeating the entire purpose of the savings plan.

blocks.title: Nigerian Market — Education Insurance in Nigeria — Market Reality

blocks.h: Education insurance is the single most commercially resonant life product category in Nigeria. The crisis in public education funding, the rising cost of private schools and universities, and the aspiration of Nigerian parents to fund quality education for their children create a powerful demand driver that no savings product can match. Key market data:

items.h: AXA Mansard's Educate plan is Nigeria's most popular education insurance product by number of policies. Features include robust premium waiver protection, flexible premium payment (monthly, quarterly, annually), and a guaranteed maturity benefit.
Leadway Assurance's Future Assure education plan offers a minimum monthly premium of ₦10,000 — the lowest entry point among major providers — making it accessible to middle-income earners.
Most education plans in Nigeria are structured as conventional with-profit endowments, with maturity dates set 10–18 years from inception corresponding to a child's university entry age.

The premium waiver rider is non-negotiable for education plans. Advisers who sell education insurance without ensuring the policyholder understands the premium waiver feature are failing a fundamental suitability obligation.

blocks.h: (d) Modified and Non-Profit Endowment

A non-profit (non-participating) endowment provides a fixed, guaranteed maturity benefit and death benefit with no bonus additions. The premium is lower than an equivalent participating endowment, but the policyholder receives no share of the insurer's investment surplus. Non-profit endowments are appropriate where the policyholder needs to plan for a specific, predetermined sum (such as a known future liability) and cannot afford the risk of bonus variations.

A modified endowment is one where the premium-paying period is shorter than the policy term (e.g. premiums paid for 10 years but cover and savings continue for 20 years). The structure is similar to limited-payment whole life but with a defined maturity date. Modified endowments are particularly attractive to business professionals who wish to fund a large capital commitment in a specific year — the premium intensity of the shorter payment period builds the cash value faster, and the maturity lump sum arrives when planned.

The anticipated endowment — universally known in Nigeria as the 'money-back policy' — is a variant of the conventional endowment that pays periodic survival benefits during the policy term in addition to the maturity benefit. These interim survival benefits are 'anticipated' from the final maturity sum, in the sense that the policyholder receives portions of their savings before the policy matures. The defining and remarkable feature of this product is that the full death benefit remains payable throughout the term regardless of how many survival benefits have already been paid.

A life assurance policy that pays periodic survival benefits (typically 20–25% of the sum assured) at defined intervals during the policy term, with the remaining sum assured plus bonuses payable at maturity. The full sum assured is payable on death throughout the term regardless of survival benefits already received. The policy combines the forced-savings discipline of an endowment with the liquidity of periodic payouts and the certainty of full death cover throughout.
Also known as: 'Money-back plan,' 'cash-back policy,' 'anticipated endowment assurance.' Dominant in the Nigerian and Indian life insurance retail markets.

blocks.h: Consider a 20-year anticipated endowment policy with a sum assured of ₦2 million on the life of Emeka, aged 35. The policy pays survival benefits of 20% of sum assured at the end of years 5, 10, and 15, with the remaining 40% plus accrued bonuses payable at maturity (year 20).

blocks.h: Key insight: Unlike a conventional savings account or fixed deposit, Emeka receives his interim payments without reducing his death benefit. If he dies in year 12 (having already received ₦800,000 in survival benefits), his family still receives the full ₦2 million sum assured plus bonuses. This 'full cover always' feature, combined with the forced savings discipline and the visible return of survival benefits, is the product's commercial strength.

The trade-off: Because the survival benefits reduce the insurer's net risk (it pays out a portion of the sum assured during the term to all surviving policyholders regardless of mortality), the premium for a money-back policy is slightly higher than an equivalent conventional endowment. The policyholder pays a modest premium for the liquidity benefit.

blocks.text: 6.5.2  Why the Money-Back Policy Dominates the Nigerian Market

blocks.h: The anticipated endowment's dominance in the Nigerian retail life market is not accidental — it reflects a deep understanding of the Nigerian consumer's financial psychology and economic reality. Three factors explain its market position:

items.h: The 'something to show' imperative: Nigerian policyholders have a well-documented resistance to products that pay nothing unless a loss occurs. The periodic survival benefits of the money-back policy provide visible, tangible returns during the policy term. Policyholders can point to the survival benefit payments as proof that 'the insurance is working,' making them far more likely to maintain the policy through its full term.

Liquidity in an illiquid market: Nigeria lacks mature, accessible savings vehicles for the average household. Fixed deposits are available but require bank relationships. The money-back policy provides pre-scheduled liquidity at defined intervals — the equivalent of a scheduled savings goal payout — which aligns with Nigerian household financial cycles (school fees, business investment, rent).

The dual-purpose appeal: Every money-back policy sold is simultaneously a savings product and a protection product. The salesperson can pitch the savings angle to the financially rational buyer and the protection angle to the family-responsibility motivated buyer, without ever misrepresenting the product.

blocks.title: Advisory — Money-Back Policy — Advisory Notes for Practitioners

blocks.h: Despite its commercial dominance, the anticipated endowment has structural limitations that every practitioner must disclose to clients:

items.h: Investment return: The effective investment return on a money-back policy is typically lower than a conventional endowment with the same premium, because the survival benefit payments reduce the fund available for long-term investment. The trade-off is liquidity versus return.

Inflation exposure: The survival benefits and maturity payment are fixed in nominal terms. A ₦400,000 survival benefit in year 10 will have significantly less purchasing power than ₦400,000 today if inflation continues at Nigerian rates. Clients should be made aware of this purchasing power risk.

Early lapse consequences: Lapsing a money-back policy in the early years is particularly costly, as the policy's front-loaded expenses mean the surrender value is minimal before year 3. The survival benefits received do not offset the loss of accumulated savings if the policy lapses prematurely.

Suitability check: For clients whose primary objective is maximum death cover, pure term assurance provides more cover per naira of premium. For clients whose primary objective is long-term wealth accumulation, an investment-linked policy may provide superior returns. The money-back policy is best suited to clients with a balanced savings-and-protection objective and a preference for periodic liquidity.

blocks.h: Universal life insurance is a permanent life product that separates the three components of a conventional whole life policy — the protection element (cost of insurance), the savings element (cash account), and the insurer's expense loading — and makes each transparent to the policyholder. The policyholder pays premiums into a cash accumulation account; each month, the insurer deducts the current cost of insurance and its administration charge from the account; the balance earns a credited interest rate. As long as the cash account is sufficient to cover the monthly deductions, the policy remains in force.<sup>[8]</sup>
This structure provides flexibility unavailable in conventional whole life or endowment products:

items.h: Premium flexibility: The policyholder can vary the premium within specified limits — paying more in good income years to build the cash value faster, and less (or nothing, drawing on the cash account) in difficult years.

Death benefit flexibility: The policyholder can adjust the death benefit (subject to underwriting evidence for increases) — increasing it as the family grows and reducing it as financial obligations diminish.
Transparency: The policyholder can see exactly how much of each premium payment is going to insurance costs, how much to administration, and how much is accumulating in the cash account.

blocks.text: 6.6.2  Universal Life in the Nigerian Market

blocks.h: Universal life has limited penetration in the Nigerian retail market currently, partly because of the complexity of explanation at point of sale and partly because the regulatory and actuarial infrastructure for pricing the interest-crediting mechanism is still developing. However, NIIRA 2025's product approval regime — which requires actuarial certification of all life product pricing — creates the conditions under which universal life products can be introduced with confidence that they are actuarially sound.

The product is more developed in the group and corporate segment, where the transparency of the internal charges is a selling point for informed corporate buyers who wish to understand the true cost of their employee benefit provision. Practitioners operating in the corporate segment should be familiar with universal life mechanics even if they are not yet selling it in volume.

A permanent life insurance product that unbundles the cost of insurance, expenses, and savings accumulation into separate, transparent components. The policyholder pays flexible premiums into a cash account; the insurer deducts the monthly cost of insurance and administration charges; the net cash account earns a credited interest rate. The policy remains in force as long as the cash account is positive. Provides greater flexibility than conventional whole life but requires more active management from the policyholder.

Key risk: If premiums are insufficient or the credited interest rate falls below projections, the cash account may be exhausted and the policy lapses — even if substantial premiums have been paid over many years.

blocks.text: 6.7  Variable Life and Investment-Linked Life Policies

blocks.h: Investment-linked life policies (also called variable life, unit-linked life, or ILPs) combine life assurance with direct participation in the performance of an investment fund. Unlike conventional life products (where the insurer bears the investment risk and provides guaranteed or smoothed returns), ILPs direct the policyholder's premium into designated investment funds — equities, bonds, money market, balanced — and the policy's cash value moves directly with the value of those funds. The policyholder bears the investment risk and receives the investment return, minus fund management charges.

The product's appeal is straightforward: in environments where equity markets produce strong long-term returns, the policyholder participates in those returns — potentially significantly outperforming the smoothed returns of a conventional with-profit endowment. The risk is equally clear: in down markets, the cash value falls, and the policyholder bears the loss. Unlike a participating policy, there is no smoothing and no guarantee of a minimum return.

A life assurance policy in which the savings component is invested in designated unit-linked funds (equities, bonds, money market, balanced, or sector-specific) chosen by the policyholder. The policy's cash value equals the current value of the units held in the chosen funds. The policyholder bears investment risk and receives investment returns. The life cover element (death benefit) may be a fixed sum assured or a multiple of the fund value, depending on the product structure.

Cf: Conventional endowment (insurer bears investment risk; smoothed, non-guaranteed bonus returns). ILPs are higher-risk, higher-potential-return alternatives suitable for investment-sophisticated policyholders.

The ILP mechanism operates as follows: the policyholder's premium is allocated to units in the chosen fund(s) at the prevailing unit price. Each month, units are encashed from the account to cover the cost of the life assurance element (the mortality deduction) and the insurer's administration charges. The remaining units continue to participate in the fund's performance. If the fund grows strongly, the policy's cash value grows; if the fund declines, the cash value falls.
Two key structural features differentiate ILPs in practice:

items.h: Premium allocation rate: The proportion of each premium invested in units, after deduction of the insurer's initial charges. In the Nigerian market, the premium allocation rate in the first year may be as low as 40–45% (reflecting first-year commission and establishment costs) and rises to 60–65% in subsequent years. The remainder is deducted as the insurer's charges before any units are purchased. This front-loading of charges means ILP policyholders should expect to see their policy value significantly below the total premiums paid in the early years.

Fund choice and switching: Policyholders choose from a menu of funds and may switch between funds (subject to switching rules and charges) as their risk appetite or market view changes. Major Nigerian ILP providers typically offer 3–5 fund options ranging from money market (lowest risk, lowest expected return) to pure equity (highest risk, highest expected return).

blocks.title: Nigerian Market — Investment-Linked Products in the Nigerian Market — Current Landscape

blocks.h: The ILP market in Nigeria is growing but remains a minority segment relative to the conventional endowment and money-back policy market. Key observations:

items.h: AXA Mansard's Wealth Plus returned 14% in 2024, outperforming most competitor products and positioning ILPs as a viable inflation-beating alternative to conventional savings.

Leadway Assurance's Smart Life offers a minimum monthly premium of ₦10,000 with fund options spanning money market and equity. The 'smart' positioning reflects a target of younger, digitally engaged investors.
ARM Life and Stanbic IBTC Insurance are also active in the ILP space, leveraging their parent organisations' investment management capabilities to offer competitive fund performance.

NAICOM requires that all ILP products clearly disclose: (a) the charges structure (allocation rate, mortality deduction, fund management fee, administration fee); (b) the fact that past fund performance does not guarantee future results; (c) the investment risk borne by the policyholder; and (d) the minimum holding period before the policy's charges structure produces a positive cash value relative to premiums paid.

blocks.h: A joint-life policy is a single policy covering two lives simultaneously, with the death benefit payable on the first death. It is most commonly used between spouses or business partners to provide a lump sum to the survivor on the first of the two insured deaths. The premium is calculated on the combined mortality experience of both lives.

Joint-life first-death policies are popular in the business protection context in Nigeria: two business partners who hold equal shares in a company each insure the other's life under a joint first-death policy. On the death of the first partner, the sum assured is paid to the surviving partner who uses it to purchase the deceased's shareholding from the estate — the classic 'buy-sell' agreement funded by life insurance. Without such an arrangement, the deceased partner's estate may be forced to sell the shareholding to a third party, potentially disrupting the business or introducing an unwanted co-owner.
Joint-life policies may also be written on a second-death (last-survivor) basis — discussed below.

A single life assurance policy covering two lives, with the sum assured payable on the earlier of the two deaths. Once the first death claim is paid, the policy terminates. The premium is based on the combined mortality of both lives. Widely used for spousal protection and business partner buy-sell arrangements in Nigeria.

Cf: Individual policies on each life (two separate policies, each paying on each life's death). Two individual policies provide more comprehensive cover; a joint first-death policy provides the benefit more cost-efficiently if only one payout is needed.

A last-survivor policy (also called joint-life second-death or survivorship policy) covers two lives and pays the sum assured only on the death of the last surviving life. The policy is designed for situations where a financial obligation arises only when both lives have died — most commonly where a couple holds estate assets that will attract inheritance costs or where a trust fund must be funded to support dependants after both parents are deceased.

Because the benefit is deferred until both lives have died, the probability of a claim in any given year is lower than for a single life, and the premium is accordingly lower than either a single-life policy on either life alone. This premium efficiency makes last-survivor policies particularly attractive for estate planning at the HNI level in Nigeria.

A rider is an additional benefit attached to a base life assurance policy, extending the policy's scope at an additional premium. Riders allow a policyholder to customise a base policy to meet specific needs without purchasing a separate policy. They are subject to NAICOM product approval as part of the base policy filing and must be priced actuarially in the product submission.

A critical illness (CI) rider pays a lump sum (typically equal to the sum assured, or a specified percentage of it) if the life assured is diagnosed with one of a defined list of specified serious illnesses during the policy term. Common covered conditions include cancer, heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, organ transplant, and major organ surgery. The benefit is paid on diagnosis of the specified condition, not on death.

The critical illness benefit is designed to address the financial consequences of serious illness that are distinct from and additional to the death benefit: the need for expensive medical treatment, the loss of income during illness and recovery, the cost of adapting a home or lifestyle, and the psychological benefit of financial security during a health crisis. In Nigeria, where health insurance penetration is low and out-of-pocket medical costs are high, the CI rider provides crucial financial support at the moment of a major health event.

The TPD rider pays the sum assured (or a specified percentage of it) if the life assured becomes totally and permanently disabled — permanently unable to perform their own occupation (the 'own occupation' definition) or any occupation for which they are reasonably suited by training, education, or experience (the 'any occupation' definition). The own-occupation definition is more generous to the policyholder; the any-occupation definition is more restrictive.

In Nigerian practice, the TPD rider is commonly written on the 'any occupation' basis — meaning the benefit is paid only if the life assured is incapable of any reasonable work, not merely their current occupation. Practitioners advising clients in high-income professions should negotiate for the own-occupation definition where available, to ensure that a professional disability (a surgeon who loses a hand, a pilot who loses vision in one eye) triggers the benefit even if the life assured could theoretically do a less specialised form of work.

The waiver of premium rider waives all future premium payments on the base policy if the policyholder becomes totally disabled (as defined in the rider). The policy remains fully in force with all its benefits intact — the insurer effectively pays the premiums on the policyholder's behalf for the duration of the disability. This rider is critical for any savings-type policy (endowment, education plan, whole life) where the continuity of the policy is financially important.

The education insurance context is the most compelling: if a parent taking an education endowment policy dies or becomes permanently disabled, the waiver of premium rider ensures the policy continues and the child still receives the maturity benefit. This is the single most important rider for any parent purchasing education insurance, and its absence should be treated as a material suitability gap.

The ADB rider pays an additional benefit (typically equal to the sum assured, i.e. doubling the total death benefit) if the life assured's death is caused by an accident. The benefit is payable in addition to the base policy death benefit. In some products the ADB triples the death benefit on accidental death ('triple indemnity').

The ADB rider is popular in Nigeria because road traffic accidents are a leading cause of death among working-age Nigerians, and the additional benefit can be the difference between financial recovery and long-term destitution for a surviving family. The rider is relatively inexpensive because accidental death is a relatively low probability event compared to all-cause mortality. NAICOM requires that the definition of 'accidental death' in the rider be clearly stated and that specific exclusions (self-inflicted injuries, war, aviation other than as a passenger on a commercial flight) be disclosed.

The hospital cash rider pays a daily cash benefit (a defined amount per day) for each day the life assured is admitted to a hospital as an in-patient. The purpose is to offset the additional living costs incurred during hospitalisation — transport for family members, supplementary food, out-of-pocket medical supplies — that are not covered by medical insurance. The benefit is fixed and payable without proof of actual expenditure.

Hospital cash riders are particularly valuable in the Nigerian context because the country's underfunded hospital system often requires patients and their families to purchase their own drugs, consumables, and even meals. A daily hospital cash benefit of ₦5,000 to ₦10,000 can meaningfully offset these costs.

blocks.h: Keyman insurance is a life assurance policy taken out by a business on the life of a key employee or executive whose death or disability would cause measurable financial loss to the business. The business is the proposer and policyholder; the employee is the life assured; the business is the beneficiary. The proceeds are paid to the business and are used to meet the costs directly attributable to the loss of the key person — recruiting and training a replacement, absorbing lost productivity during the transition, meeting loan obligations secured by the key person's personal guarantee.

Insurable interest is established on the basis of the economic value the key person contributes to the business — the test is the financial loss the business would sustain, not affection or personal relationship. A managing director who generates ₦200 million of annual revenue through her relationships and expertise represents an insurable economic interest of that order of magnitude. The sum assured should be calculated on a demonstrable financial basis, not arbitrarily.

A life assurance policy taken out by a business on the life of a key employee or executive, with the business as beneficiary. The purpose is to indemnify the business against the financial loss caused by the death or permanent disability of a person whose skills, relationships, or leadership are critical to the business's income-generating capacity. The sum assured is based on the demonstrable economic value of the key person to the business.

Note: Keyman insurance requires documented insurable interest — the business must demonstrate the financial relationship between the key person's services and the business's earnings. The sum assured must be actuarially and commercially justifiable. Source: Royal Exchange Prudential Life, Royal Keyman product.
Several approaches to quantifying the key person's economic value are used in practice:

items.h: Income multiple approach: The sum assured is set at a multiple of the key person's total annual remuneration (salary, bonuses, benefits) — typically 5 to 10 times. The rationale is that this multiple represents the expected cost of recruiting, onboarding, and losing productivity during the transition to a replacement of equivalent capability.

Revenue contribution approach: Where the key person is responsible for a significant proportion of the business's revenue — a sales director, a founding partner with client relationships — the sum assured is set at a multiple of their revenue contribution.
Loan and guarantee coverage: Where the key person has personally guaranteed business loans, the sum assured should at minimum cover the outstanding loan balances guaranteed by the individual.

Replacement cost approach: The sum assured is calculated as the total cost of replacing the key person: executive search fees, sign-on bonuses for a replacement, training costs, and the cost of lost business during the transition period.

blocks.h: NAICOM's underwriting guidelines require that keyman insurance proposals above a specified sum threshold include a financial justification signed by an authorised officer of the company and certified by the company's auditors. This requirement prevents over-insurance and addresses the insurable interest question definitively at the underwriting stage.

blocks.text: 6.11  Mortgage Protection and Credit Life Insurance

blocks.h: Mortgage protection insurance is a life policy specifically designed to repay an outstanding mortgage or property loan on the death (or, in some products, the permanent disability) of the borrower. The policy is typically structured as a decreasing term assurance with a sum assured that mirrors the reducing outstanding mortgage balance. The mortgagee (the bank or lender) is named as the assignee and receives the proceeds directly, which are applied to settle the outstanding debt.

In Nigeria, mortgage protection insurance is becoming increasingly important as the National Housing Fund and commercial mortgage products from the federal mortgage bank and commercial lenders generate a growing stock of long-term property debt. NIIRA 2025 does not yet mandate mortgage protection insurance, but many lenders require it as a condition of mortgage approval, and the structural parallel with the credit life mandate (discussed below) suggests that mandatory mortgage cover may be a future regulatory development.

blocks.text: 6.11.2  Credit Life Insurance — The NIIRA 2025 Mandate

blocks.h: Credit life insurance is a life policy that covers an outstanding debt — typically a personal loan, business loan, or hire purchase obligation — against the death or permanent disability of the borrower. On the occurrence of the insured event, the insurance benefit is used to repay the outstanding balance, protecting the borrower's family or estate from inheriting the debt. NIIRA 2025 introduces a significant statutory obligation in this area:<sup>[15]</sup><sup>[20]</sup>

blocks.title: Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Mandatory Credit Life Insurance for Loans Exceeding ₦10 Million

blocks.h: Section 91(3) of NIIRA 2025 establishes the following requirements:

items.h: All credit providers (banks, microfinance banks, fintechs, and other lenders) must require borrowers who take out loans exceeding ₦10 million to obtain credit life insurance before the loan is disbursed.
The credit life policy must cover the remaining balance of the loan if the borrower dies or becomes permanently disabled.

The lender is named as the beneficiary in the policy to the extent of the outstanding loan balance. Any excess benefit (where the sum assured exceeds the outstanding debt at the time of claim) is paid to the borrower's estate or named beneficiary.
The cost of the credit life insurance must be transparently disclosed to the borrower at the time of the loan offer. Hidden insurance charges bundled into loan fees without disclosure are prohibited.
Lenders who disburse loans exceeding ₦10 million without ensuring credit life insurance is in place are in breach of NIIRA 2025 and face regulatory sanctions from NAICOM.

blocks.h: The credit life mandate is significant for two reasons: it dramatically expands the market for credit life insurance in Nigeria (the ₦10 million threshold captures a wide range of business loans, personal loans, and mortgage products), and it brings life insurance into the fintech and digital lending space for the first time with regulatory force. Life insurers should be developing API-enabled credit life products that can be embedded in digital lending platforms, consistent with the Insurtech licensing framework in NAICOM's August 2025 Guidelines.

blocks.text: 6.12  Product Suitability: Matching Products to Client Needs

blocks.h: The CIIN Code of Ethics and NIIRA 2025's market conduct provisions both require that insurance products are sold only to clients for whom they are suitable. Suitability analysis in life insurance requires the practitioner to assess the client's financial needs, objectives, income, existing insurance arrangements, risk appetite, and time horizon — and to match those characteristics to the product most likely to serve the client's genuine interests.

No single product is universally superior. The 'best' life insurance product for any client is the one that most closely aligns their protection needs, savings objectives, premium affordability, and time horizon. A 28-year-old with young children and a large mortgage has fundamentally different needs from a 55-year-old business owner planning estate transfer.

blocks.title: Advisory — Product Suitability — Practitioner Obligations under NIIRA 2025

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 and the CIIN Code of Ethics impose clear suitability obligations on all licensed intermediaries:

items.h: Know Your Client (KYC): Before making any product recommendation, the practitioner must collect sufficient information about the client's financial situation, objectives, existing cover, and risk tolerance to enable a genuine suitability assessment.

Document the recommendation: The basis for the product recommendation must be documented and retained. If the client declines a recommended product in favour of an alternative, the client's decision must be recorded.

Disclose non-guaranteed elements: All bonus projections, fund performance illustrations, and projected maturity values must be clearly labelled as projections, not guarantees. The guaranteed minimum benefit must be separately stated.
Disclose charges fully: All first-year charges, ongoing management fees, and exit costs must be disclosed before the client commits to the policy.

Mis-selling consequences: NIIRA 2025 empowers NAICOM to sanction intermediaries found to have mis-sold insurance products — through unsuitable recommendations, misrepresentation of benefits, concealment of charges, or pressure-selling. Sanctions include fines, suspension of licence, and in cases of deliberate fraud, criminal prosecution.

blocks.h: This chapter has surveyed the full range of life insurance product types available in Nigeria and internationally. The following are the chapter's essential propositions.

items.h: Term assurance is the purest and most cost-efficient form of life cover, providing a death benefit only if the life assured dies within the specified term. Variants include level, decreasing, increasing, return-of-premium, renewable, and convertible term, each serving a distinct financial purpose.

Whole life assurance provides lifetime cover with no expiry date, accumulating a cash value over time. Variants include ordinary level-premium, limited-payment, and single-premium whole life. Participating whole life earns reversionary and terminal bonuses; non-participating whole life provides a fixed guaranteed benefit.

Endowment assurance combines protection and savings: the sum assured is payable on death or on survival to maturity. Variants include conventional with-profit endowment, pure endowment (survival only), educational endowment with premium waiver, and modified/non-profit endowment.

The anticipated endowment ('money-back policy') dominates the Nigerian retail life market. It pays periodic survival benefits during the term (typically 20% of sum assured at 5-year intervals) while maintaining the full death benefit throughout. Its commercial success reflects Nigerian consumers' preference for visible returns and periodic liquidity.

Universal life separates the cost of insurance, expenses, and savings accumulation into transparent, flexible components. The policyholder can vary premiums and death benefit within limits. It is more complex than conventional products and requires active policyholder management.

Investment-linked (unit-linked) policies direct the savings component into designated investment funds. The policyholder bears investment risk and receives market returns. In Nigeria, equity-linked ILPs have produced 10–14% returns in recent years, outperforming conventional endowments. Front-loaded charges mean ILPs require a long holding period to achieve positive cash value.

Joint-life first-death policies cover two lives and pay on the first death. Last-survivor (second-death) policies pay only when both lives have died. Both are important in business protection and estate planning.

Key riders include critical illness, total and permanent disability, waiver of premium, accidental death benefit, and hospital cash. Riders extend the policy's scope to cover specific risks without requiring a separate policy. The waiver of premium rider is non-negotiable for education endowment policies.

Keyman insurance protects a business against the financial loss caused by the death or disability of a key employee. The sum assured must be justified by a demonstrable economic interest. The buy-sell business protection arrangement is a key application.

Credit life insurance covers an outstanding debt against the borrower's death or disability. NIIRA 2025, Section 91(3), mandates credit life insurance for all loans exceeding ₦10 million — a requirement that opens a major new market for life insurers in the banking and fintech lending space.

Product suitability requires matching product features to each client's protection needs, savings objectives, premium affordability, and time horizon. NIIRA 2025 and the CIIN Code of Ethics impose specific obligations to document suitability assessments, disclose non-guaranteed elements, and avoid mis-selling.

blocks.h: A life insurance policy providing a death benefit only if the life assured dies within a specified term. No benefit is payable on survival. No savings element or cash value.
Term assurance with a fixed sum assured and fixed premium throughout the policy term. The most common term structure.
Term assurance with a sum assured that reduces over the policy term, mirroring the reducing balance of a debt obligation. Premiums are typically level.
Term assurance with a sum assured that increases over the term, typically for inflation protection.
Term assurance with a clause entitling the policyholder to renew at the end of the term without fresh medical evidence, at a premium based on attained age.
Term assurance with a clause entitling the policyholder to convert to a permanent product before the term expires without fresh medical evidence.
Permanent life cover with no expiry date, providing a guaranteed death benefit whenever death occurs, as long as premiums are paid.
Whole life with premiums compressed into a shorter period (e.g. 20 years) after which no further premiums are required but cover continues for life.
Whole life funded by one lump-sum premium at inception. Immediate cash value. Used for estate planning and wealth transfer.
Pays the sum assured on death during the term or on survival to maturity — whichever occurs first. Combines savings and protection.
Pays only on survival to maturity; no benefit on prior death. A savings vehicle. Embedded in annuity pricing.
An endowment designed to fund a child's education, maturing at the expected university entry date, with a mandatory premium waiver rider.
An endowment paying periodic survival benefits during the term (typically 20% of sum assured at 5-year intervals) plus the remaining sum assured at maturity. Full death cover maintained throughout.
Permanent life insurance that separates cost of insurance, administration, and savings into transparent, flexible components. The policyholder can vary premiums and death benefit within limits.
Life assurance where the savings element is invested in designated funds. The policyholder bears investment risk and receives market returns. Also called unit-linked or variable life.
A single policy covering two lives; the sum assured is paid on the first death. Used for spousal protection and business partner buy-sell arrangements.
A policy covering two lives; the sum assured is paid only on the death of the last survivor. Used for estate planning and trust funding.
An additional benefit paying a lump sum on diagnosis of a specified serious illness during the policy term.
Total and Permanent Disability rider. Pays a lump sum on total and permanent incapacity. 'Own occupation' vs 'any occupation' definitions critically affect coverage scope.
Waives all future premiums on the base policy if the policyholder becomes totally disabled. Non-negotiable for education insurance policies.
Pays an additional death benefit (equal to or a multiple of the sum assured) if death is caused by an accident. Cost-effective in Nigeria given high road traffic mortality.
Life assurance taken out by a business on a key employee's life, with the business as beneficiary, to compensate for the financial loss caused by the key person's death or disability.
Life assurance that covers an outstanding loan balance against the borrower's death or permanent disability. Mandatory under NIIRA 2025 for loans exceeding ₦10 million.
Life assurance designed to repay an outstanding mortgage on the borrower's death. Typically structured as decreasing term with the lender as assignee.
